subtopic_detail: First line treatment of asymptomatic hypoglycaemia in an at risk newborn
stem:
You are the paediatric resident called to the postnatal ward to see a two hour old boy born at 39 weeks and 1 day to a mother whose gestational diabetes was managed with metformin. His birth weight is 4250 g and he had a good breastfeed at 40 minutes of age.

He is pink and alert with normal tone, is not jittery, and has no grunting, tachypnoea or recession. His axillary temperature is 36.9 degrees Celsius and he is rooting for a further feed. The routine pre feed blood glucose taken by the midwife is 2.2 mmol/L, confirmed on a laboratory sample.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 138 beats per minute, respiratory rate 46 breaths per minute, SpO2 98 per cent on room air, temperature 36.9 degrees Celsius
data_table.Investigations: Blood glucose 2.2 mmol/L on a laboratory confirmed sample, taken before the second feed
data_table.Examination: Alert, pink, normal tone, no jitteriness, anterior fontanelle soft, cardiovascular and respiratory examination normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Give buccal 40 per cent dextrose gel and support a breastfeed
options.rationale: Buccal dextrose gel with a feed is first line for asymptomatic hypoglycaemia in an at risk newborn, reduces admission to special care and does not interfere with establishing breastfeeding (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal Hypoglycaemia).

options.text: Give a 2 mL/kg bolus of 10 per cent glucose intravenously now
options.rationale: An intravenous bolus is reserved for a symptomatic infant or one with a blood glucose below about 1.5 mmol/L, and it separates a well baby from his mother unnecessarily (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal Hypoglycaemia).

options.text: Give a formula top up by bottle and recheck the glucose in one hour
options.rationale: Feeding alone raises the glucose more slowly than gel plus a feed, and introducing a bottle at two hours of age undermines breastfeeding when an equally effective option exists (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal Hypoglycaemia).

options.text: Recheck the blood glucose before the next feed without treating now
options.rationale: A confirmed value below 2.6 mmol/L in an at risk infant requires treatment rather than observation, because neuroglycopenic injury can occur before clinical signs appear (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal Hypoglycaemia).

options.text: Admit to the special care nursery for an intravenous glucose infusion
options.rationale: Nursery admission with an infusion is for persistent or symptomatic hypoglycaemia that has not responded to gel and feeds, and it is not the first step in a well feeding baby (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal Hypoglycaemia).

explanation.summary: Newborns at risk of hypoglycaemia include infants of diabetic mothers, those who are large or small for gestational age, preterm infants and those who are unwell, and these babies are screened with pre feed glucose measurements in the first 24 hours. The Australian operational threshold is 2.6 mmol/L, chosen because it is the level below which neurophysiological changes have been demonstrated rather than because symptoms appear there. Dextrose gel changed practice because it treats effectively without separating mother and baby, and it is given at 0.5 mL per kilogram rubbed into the buccal mucosa, followed immediately by a feed and a repeat glucose 30 minutes later. Failure to respond after two doses, symptoms, or a very low reading move the infant onto the intravenous pathway, and hypoglycaemia persisting beyond 48 to 72 hours prompts investigation for hyperinsulinism or an endocrine cause.
key_points: The Australian operational threshold for newborn hypoglycaemia is 2.6 mmol/L
Dextrose gel 0.5 mL per kilogram buccally plus a feed is first line
Recheck the glucose 30 minutes after the gel is given
Intravenous glucose is for symptomatic infants or failure of gel and feeds
Hypoglycaemia persisting past 48 to 72 hours needs endocrine investigation
explanation.pearls: When hypoglycaemia persists beyond 72 hours, take a critical sample at the time of a low glucose for insulin, cortisol, growth hormone, ketones and free fatty acids, because the diagnosis of hyperinsulinism depends on measuring insulin while the glucose is actually low.

subtopic_detail: First line drug choice in a generalised epilepsy where one common agent is aggravating
stem:
You are the general paediatric registrar seeing a 6 year old girl whose teacher has recorded 20 to 30 episodes a day in which she stops mid sentence, stares, and does not respond for a few seconds before carrying on as if nothing happened. Her school work has fallen away this term.

She does not fall, does not jerk and is not drowsy or confused afterwards. When you ask her to blow on a paper windmill for two minutes in clinic she stops and stares for six seconds with fluttering eyelids and a brief upward eye movement. Her development, growth and neurological examination are normal, and an electroencephalogram shows generalised 3 Hz spike and wave discharges on a normal background.

data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, electrolytes, calcium and glucose within normal limits
data_table.Electroencephalogram: Generalised symmetrical 3 Hz spike and wave discharges on a normal background, provoked by hyperventilation

lead_in: What is the most appropriate treatment?

options.text: Commence carbamazepine and review the seizure diary in four weeks
options.rationale: Carbamazepine aggravates absence seizures and can precipitate absence status, making it a specifically contraindicated choice in generalised epilepsies (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology).

options.text: Commence ethosuximide and review the seizure diary in four weeks
options.rationale: Ethosuximide is first line for childhood absence epilepsy, with a comparative trial showing equal seizure freedom to valproate but less attentional impairment and fewer adverse effects (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology; RCH CPG: Afebrile Seizures).

options.text: Commence levetiracetam and review the seizure diary in four weeks
options.rationale: Levetiracetam is markedly less effective for typical absence seizures than ethosuximide or valproate and is not a first line choice in this syndrome (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology).

options.text: Commence lamotrigine and review the seizure diary in four weeks
options.rationale: Lamotrigine is effective in generalised epilepsy but requires slow titration over weeks and achieved lower seizure freedom rates than ethosuximide in the comparative trial (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology).

options.text: Arrange brain magnetic resonance imaging before starting treatment
options.rationale: Neuroimaging is not required when the clinical syndrome and electroencephalogram are typical, and is reserved for focal features, developmental regression or an abnormal examination (Source: RCH CPG: Afebrile Seizures).

explanation.summary: Childhood absence epilepsy typically begins between four and ten years of age in a developmentally normal child and is defined by frequent brief staring episodes without postictal confusion, accompanied by generalised 3 Hz spike and wave activity. Hyperventilation for two to three minutes provokes an event in the great majority of untreated children, which makes it the single most useful bedside test and is often achieved by asking the child to blow a windmill or a tissue. The differential is inattention or daydreaming, which is not interruptible in the same way and does not stop mid activity, and focal impaired awareness seizures, which have an aura, automatisms and postictal drowsiness. Prognosis is good with around two thirds achieving remission by adolescence, though attentional difficulties can persist and warrant follow up even after seizures stop.
key_points: Hyperventilation provokes an absence in most untreated children
There is no aura and no postictal confusion in typical absence seizures
Carbamazepine, phenytoin, gabapentin and vigabatrin aggravate absence seizures
Neuroimaging is not needed when syndrome and electroencephalogram are typical
Attentional difficulties can persist after seizure remission
explanation.pearls: In the randomised comparison of the three first line agents, ethosuximide and valproate both achieved around 45 per cent freedom from failure at 12 months against 21 per cent for lamotrigine, and ethosuximide caused less attentional impairment than valproate.

subtopic_detail: Timing of referral for a palpable inguinal testis that has never been in the scrotum
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 14 month old boy for a routine check. His mother mentions that a doctor told her at the six week check that one of his testes was not down, and she was told it would probably sort itself out.

The right hemiscrotum is small and empty. You can feel a firm mobile testis in the right inguinal canal and can bring it as far as the neck of the scrotum, but it springs straight back when you let go. The left testis sits normally in the scrotum, the phallus is normal with a terminal meatus, and his growth and general examination are normal.

data_table.Examination: Empty right hemiscrotum with a palpable testis in the right inguinal canal that cannot be brought into the scrotum, normally descended left testis, normal phallus with terminal meatus
data_table.Growth: Weight and length tracking along the 50th centile

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Reassure the parents and review the testis at his second birthday
options.rationale: Spontaneous descent essentially never occurs after six months of corrected age, so further waiting only delays surgery past the recommended window (Source: RCH CPG: Undescended Testis).

options.text: Arrange an ultrasound of the groin to locate the testis first
options.rationale: Imaging adds nothing when the testis is already palpable, and ultrasound has poor sensitivity for a truly impalpable testis so it does not change management either way (Source: RCH CPG: Undescended Testis).

options.text: Refer to paediatric surgery for orchidopexy without further delay
options.rationale: A testis that has never been in the scrotum and cannot be brought there requires orchidopexy, ideally completed between six and twelve months of age, so at 14 months referral should be immediate (Source: RCH CPG: Undescended Testis).

options.text: Arrange human chorionic gonadotrophin stimulation before referral
options.rationale: Hormonal treatment has low success rates, a high relapse rate and is not used in Australian practice for an isolated unilateral undescended testis (Source: RCH CPG: Undescended Testis).

options.text: Refer for karyotype and hormonal testing before any surgical opinion
options.rationale: Endocrine and genetic assessment is indicated for bilateral impalpable testes or for hypospadias with an undescended testis, because those combinations raise the possibility of a difference of sex development, and neither applies here (Source: RCH CPG: Undescended Testis).

explanation.summary: Around 3 per cent of term boys have an undescended testis at birth and most descend spontaneously by three months of corrected age, after which further descent is very unlikely. The main clinical task is distinguishing a true undescended testis from a retractile one, which can be brought into the scrotum and stays there until the cremasteric reflex fires again, and which needs annual review rather than surgery. Orchidopexy is recommended between six and twelve months of age because the germ cell population deteriorates from the second year, and earlier surgery is associated with better fertility outcomes and a lower risk of malignancy. Surgery does not abolish the increased risk of testicular cancer but does make the testis examinable, which is why these boys are taught testicular self examination from adolescence.
key_points: Spontaneous descent is very unlikely after six months of corrected age
A retractile testis stays in the scrotum once brought there and needs review only
Orchidopexy is recommended between six and twelve months of age
Ultrasound does not help for either a palpable or an impalpable testis
Bilateral impalpable testes or associated hypospadias warrant endocrine assessment
explanation.pearls: Examine for an undescended testis with warm hands and the child relaxed, sweeping from the anterior superior iliac spine along the inguinal canal towards the scrotum, because a cold room or a cold hand triggers the cremasteric reflex and turns a normal testis into an apparently undescended one.

sources.label: Urological Society of Australia and New Zealand

subtopic_detail: Selecting first line treatment for primary monosymptomatic nocturnal enuresis
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 7 year old boy who wets the bed five or six nights a week and has never been dry for longer than a fortnight. He has started refusing invitations to sleep at his cousin's house and tells you he wants it to stop.

He is dry all day, has no urgency or frequency, and does not have to rush to the toilet. He opens his bowels once a day with a soft stool and has never soiled. His growth, abdominal examination, spine and lower limb neurological examination are normal, and his parents say they are willing to be woken at night and to keep a record.

data_table.Investigations: Urinalysis shows no glucose, protein, blood, nitrites or leucocytes
data_table.Examination: Normal abdominal examination with no palpable faecal loading, normal lumbosacral spine and normal lower limb neurological examination

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first line treatment?

options.text: Prescribe desmopressin each night and review him in three months
options.rationale: Desmopressin works quickly but relapse on stopping is common, so it is chosen for short term cover such as a camp or when alarm therapy is not feasible rather than as first line (Source: RCH CPG: Enuresis).

options.text: Advise no drinks after six in the evening and review in three months
options.rationale: Evening fluid restriction alone has not been shown to cure enuresis and can lead to daytime under drinking with reduced functional bladder capacity (Source: RCH CPG: Enuresis).

options.text: Prescribe oxybutynin twice daily and review him in three months
options.rationale: Anticholinergics are for overactive bladder with daytime urgency and frequency, and this boy has no daytime symptoms at all (Source: RCH CPG: Enuresis).

options.text: Arrange an enuresis alarm and review him after four to six weeks
options.rationale: Alarm therapy is first line for primary monosymptomatic nocturnal enuresis in a motivated child over six years with engaged parents, achieving lasting dryness in around two thirds with a much lower relapse rate than drug treatment (Source: RCH CPG: Enuresis).

options.text: Prescribe imipramine at night and review him after four to six weeks
options.rationale: Tricyclic antidepressants are a last resort for refractory enuresis because of cardiotoxicity in overdose and a high relapse rate on cessation (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook).

explanation.summary: Nocturnal enuresis affects around 15 per cent of five year olds and resolves spontaneously in about 15 per cent of affected children each year, so treatment is offered when the child is bothered rather than at a fixed age. The first step is separating monosymptomatic enuresis from enuresis with daytime symptoms, since the latter points to bladder dysfunction and needs a different approach, and the second is excluding and treating constipation, which is the commonest reversible contributor. Urinalysis is done once to exclude diabetes mellitus, diabetes insipidus and urinary infection, and further imaging is not required in a child with a normal examination. Alarm therapy works by conditioning and takes several weeks to have effect, so families need to be told at the outset to persist for at least six weeks and to continue until 14 consecutive dry nights are achieved.
key_points: Separate monosymptomatic enuresis from enuresis with daytime symptoms
Exclude and treat constipation before starting specific treatment
Urinalysis is the only routine investigation needed
Alarm therapy is first line and has the lowest relapse rate
Desmopressin is useful for short term cover such as camps and sleepovers
explanation.pearls: Continue alarm therapy until the child has achieved 14 consecutive dry nights, usually around eight to twelve weeks in total, because stopping at the first run of dry nights is the commonest cause of relapse.

subtopic_detail: Follow up schedule for renal involvement after a childhood small vessel vasculitis
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar reviewing a 6 year old boy who has had a raised purple rash over his buttocks and the backs of both legs for five days, along with sore swollen ankles and tummy pain that comes and goes.

The rash does not fade when you press it and the spots stand up from the skin. His abdomen is soft with no guarding and no mass, his stool has tested negative for blood and his scrotum is not swollen or tender. He is eating and drinking, walking with a limp, and his parents want to know what happens next.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 96 beats per minute, blood pressure 98/60 mmHg, respiratory rate 22 breaths per minute, SpO2 99 per cent on room air, temperature 36.9 degrees Celsius
data_table.Investigations: Platelets 380 x10^9/L (150-450), haemoglobin 124 g/L (110-145), international normalised ratio 1.0, activated partial thromboplastin time within normal limits, creatinine 34 micromol/L (20-60), albumin 38 g/L (35-50)
data_table.Urinalysis: Blood 1 plus, protein negative, no nitrites or leucocytes

lead_in: What is the most appropriate ongoing plan?

options.text: Commence oral prednisolone for one week and then review him
options.rationale: Corticosteroids are used for severe abdominal pain or orchitis and do not prevent or treat the renal involvement, so they are not given for isolated haematuria (Source: RCH CPG: Henoch Schonlein Purpura).

options.text: Refer for renal biopsy before the rash begins to resolve
options.rationale: Biopsy is indicated for nephrotic range proteinuria, impaired renal function or a rapidly progressive course, none of which is present with isolated microscopic haematuria (Source: RCH CPG: Henoch Schonlein Purpura).

options.text: Commence an angiotensin converting enzyme inhibitor today
options.rationale: Angiotensin blockade is used for established persistent proteinuria rather than for haematuria alone, and starting it now would treat a complication that has not developed (Source: RCH CPG: Henoch Schonlein Purpura).

options.text: Discharge with advice to return only if the rash worsens
options.rationale: Renal involvement can appear weeks after the rash has faded and is silent until it is advanced, so discharge without surveillance is the error that allows nephritis to be missed (Source: RCH CPG: Henoch Schonlein Purpura).

options.text: Arrange weekly urinalysis and blood pressure for one month
options.rationale: Australian practice is weekly urinalysis and blood pressure for the first month, then at decreasing frequency for six to twelve months, because nephritis develops in around a third of children and almost always within the first six months (Source: RCH CPG: Henoch Schonlein Purpura).

explanation.summary: Immunoglobulin A vasculitis is the commonest vasculitis of childhood and is diagnosed clinically on palpable purpura in a gravity dependent distribution with at least one of arthritis or arthralgia, abdominal pain, renal involvement or a compatible biopsy. A normal platelet count and normal coagulation are what separate it from thrombocytopenic and coagulopathic causes of purpura, and they should be checked in every child. The rash and joint symptoms settle over weeks, but renal involvement is the determinant of long term outcome and is the reason these children need structured follow up rather than simple discharge. Intussusception is the other complication to warn parents about, since it is typically ileoileal in this condition and may not be visible on the ultrasound views used for the usual ileocolic form.
key_points: Diagnosis is clinical, with palpable purpura in a gravity dependent distribution
Normal platelets and coagulation separate it from other causes of purpura
Nephritis develops in about a third and almost always within six months
Corticosteroids treat severe abdominal pain but do not prevent nephritis
Warn parents about intussusception, which is usually ileoileal in this condition
explanation.pearls: Continue urinalysis and blood pressure surveillance for at least six months after the rash resolves, because late nephritis presenting after the first month accounts for a substantial minority of cases and is entirely asymptomatic until proteinuria is heavy.
